title: Respirators, fit testing and health monitoring
audience: Stone and terrazzo restoration workers, leading hands and supervisors who choose, issue and check respiratory protection
learningOutcomes: Explain why respiratory protection is the last control for stone dust
Describe when a worker must pass a fit test before wearing a tight-fitting respirator
Explain when health monitoring must be arranged and who pays for it under the guidance
referencesAtStart: NT WorkSafe, Guide to working with crystalline silica and crystalline silica containing products, version 1.1 (29 January 2026), confirmed for the Northern Territory; NSW Resources Regulator, Position paper: regulatory approach to crystalline silica regulation (April 2025), confirmed as a position paper for mine and petroleum operators, not as a general rule.

instruction.heading: Respiratory protection is the last line
instruction.body: Respiratory protective equipment comes after the engineering controls described in “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”. Some risk can remain after those controls are in place, and a respirator is then needed for that residual risk. The national guidance of February 2022 ranks personal protective equipment last in the control order. It places this kind of protection at the weakest end of the ranking and warns against leaning on it by itself. For processing porcelain, sintered stone or engineered stone, the NT WorkSafe guide puts the duty on the business to supply breathing protection to everyone who may be exposed, and says the worker must keep it on for the whole of the processing work. The NT guide is a Northern Territory document, so its duty applies in the Northern Territory. Choose the respirator from a documented risk assessment, not from habit, from a product on a shelf, or from what the worker used on a previous job.

instruction.heading: Choosing the respirator and the standard
instruction.body: The respirator's type, class, filter and standard must match the task and the manufacturer's data. The NT guide names two Australian and New Zealand standards for respiratory protective equipment used in processing porcelain, sintered stone and engineered stone: AS/NZS 1716:2012 and AS/NZS 1715:2009. Those are the standards the NT guide names. A respirator that meets a standard is still only suitable if its class, filter and fit suit the task. Record the choice against the risk assessment, with the model, the class and the filter, and keep the manufacturer's data on file. Do not state them as a requirement for another jurisdiction.

instruction.heading: Fit testing comes before first use
instruction.body: A respirator protects only if it seals to the face. The national guidance expects a worker to pass a fit test before first wearing a tight-fitting respirator. The guidance also expects a repeat test after a change of make or model, after a change in facial features, and once a year at least. The guidance prefers a quantitative test for full face and powered types. A qualitative test, which depends on the wearer detecting a taste or odour, is for half-face types only, because it can give a misleading pass for the other types.A fit test is specific to a model, a size and a person, so a changed model or size needs a new test. The NT guide also expects a fit check every time the respirator goes on. Facial hair, glasses and damaged seals can defeat the seal, so the fit-test provider's instructions and the manufacturer's directions apply.

instruction.heading: Health monitoring is a duty, not a choice
instruction.body: The national guidance expects monitoring to begin as soon as someone takes on silica work, whether at hire or when they move onto such tasks, so that early changes in health are picked up. For people already working with these materials without monitoring, the guidance asks for arrangements to be put in place promptly. In the Northern Territory, the NT WorkSafe guide puts on the business the duty to arrange and fund monitoring where silica exposure poses a risk to health. That duty is not limited to the people who create the dust. The NT guide also reaches those who clean up the work area and the tools. The NSW Resources Regulator position paper of April 2025 deals with monitoring for high-risk processing, but its context is mine and petroleum operators, and it is a position paper rather than the regulation itself. The decision to monitor depends on the risk and the work done, not on how long the job lasts. Arrange monitoring through a qualified provider, keep the arrangement on file, and do not attempt to assess a worker's health on the job.

instruction.heading: Stop-work and the start of a dusty task
instruction.body: A dusty task does not start until the controls before it are in place. For a tight-fitting respirator, that means a current fit test for the model and size, a seal check on the day, training in fitting, checking, cleaning and storage, and a monitoring arrangement on file where the risk requires one. If any of these is missing, the worker does not start the dusty task. The worker can take up a non-dusty task, such as setting up the water feed or the barriers, while the supervisor puts the missing record in place. Record the stop, the reason and the date it is lifted.

procedure: Confirm the residual risk that remains after the engineering controls in “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping” are in place and checked.
Select the respirator type, class and filter from the documented risk assessment and the manufacturer's data.
Confirm which standard applies in the state or territory of the work, and do not state a standard as a requirement until it is confirmed.
Confirm that the worker has a current fit test for that model and size before the first use, and that the test was carried out by the method the guidance recommends for that respirator type.
Check that the worker has been trained in fitting, seal checking, cleaning and storing the respirator, and that the training is recorded.
Carry out a user seal check each time the respirator is put on, as the manufacturer directs.
Confirm that health monitoring is arranged through a qualified provider where the risk requires it, and record the date of the arrangement.
If any fit test, training or monitoring arrangement is missing, the worker does not start the dusty task. Record the stop and the reason.

workedExamples.situation: A new employee joins a polishing crew on the first day and asks to start straight away. They have a disposable dust mask bought from a hardware store and say they have worn one on other jobs.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the employee start the dusty task, and what must happen first?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The respirator has not been chosen from a documented risk assessment, there is no fit test for the model and size, and no training is recorded. Respiratory protection is the last control, so the engineering controls must be in place and checked first. The employee can work on a non-dusty task, such as setting up the water feed or the barriers. Before any dusty task, the supervisor arranges a fit test for the chosen respirator, training in fitting, seal checking, cleaning and storage, and the monitoring arrangement where the risk requires it. The employee starts the dusty task only after those records exist. The mask the employee brought in is not a substitute for a chosen and tested respirator.

workedExamples.situation: A worker's tight-fitting respirator is replaced with a different model of the same size, because the first model is out of stock.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can the worker wear the new model on the same day, and what record is needed?
workedExamples.reasoning: Not until the worker has been fit tested on the new model. The national guidance calls for a fit test when a new make or model is issued, and a fit test is specific to the model. Record the new model, the size, the date of the new test and the provider. Keep the old record, and note the date the change took effect. The seal check before each use still applies.

equipmentAndPpe: Respirator selected from the risk assessment, with the manufacturer's data, class and filter recorded
Fit-test kit or provider's record for the specific model and size
Seal check instructions for the model, as the manufacturer directs
Cleaning and storage materials for respirators, as the manufacturer directs
Standard site PPE set by the site induction
Sharps and waste containers only where other work on the site requires them

commonErrors.error: Using a disposable dust mask chosen without a risk assessment or a fit test as the main protection.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose respiratory protection from the risk assessment and the manufacturer's data, after the engineering controls are in place, and fit test the model before use.

commonErrors.error: Skipping health monitoring because the job will be short.
commonErrors.prevention: Decide the monitoring duty on the risk and the work done, not on job length. Arrange the monitoring with a qualified provider before dusty work starts.

commonErrors.error: Assuming an old fit test covers a new respirator model or a new size.
commonErrors.prevention: A fit test is specific to the model and size. Re-test when either changes.

commonErrors.error: Treating the annual fit-test interval as optional, or treating it as settled law in every state.
commonErrors.prevention: Plan the annual re-test as the national guidance sets it, and check the legal status of the interval in the state of the work with the regulator.

commonErrors.error: Not carrying out a user seal check before each use.
commonErrors.prevention: Carry out the seal check every time the respirator is put on, as the manufacturer directs and as the NT guide expects.

commonErrors.error: Applying the NT guide's duties in another state without checking.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat the NT guide as the NT position. Check the local regulator's position before applying it elsewhere.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The national guidance of February 2022 puts this protection at the bottom of the ranking, warns against using it by itself, and expects a fit test before first use of a tight-fitting respirator. It is national guidance.

The NT guide of 29 January 2026 requires respirators to be supplied to people exposed while engineered stone is processed, and puts the arrangement and funding of health monitoring on the business where there is a risk to health. These duties are confirmed for the Northern Territory.

The NT guide names AS/NZS 1716:2012 and AS/NZS 1715:2009 for respiratory protective equipment for processing engineered stone. Completing this lesson does not certify any worker as fit to wear a respirator, and it does not approve any respirator model.
The NSW Resources Regulator position paper of April 2025 concerns mine and petroleum operators and is a position paper, not regulation.

qualityStandard: Every worker who wears a tight-fitting respirator has a current fit test for that model and size.
Respirator selection, including its class and filter, is recorded against the risk assessment.
Health monitoring arrangements are on file before dusty work starts where the risk requires them.
Training is recorded for each worker who fits, checks, cleans and stores a respirator.
Every stop caused by a missing fit test, training or monitoring record is recorded with the date it was lifted.
documentationEvidence: Respirator selection record linked to the risk assessment, with model, class and filter
Fit-test record with date, model, size, method and provider
Training record for fitting, seal checking, cleaning and storage
Health monitoring arrangement and date, held by the business
Stop record for any dusty task that did not start, with the reason and the date it was lifted
summary: Respiratory protection is the last control, not the first, and it is never the only control.
Fit test each model and size before first use, and re-test when the model or size changes or when facial characteristics change.
The national guidance expects a re-test at least once a year.
Do a user seal check every time the respirator is put on.
Health monitoring is a duty where the risk exists. Arrange it before dusty work starts.
The NT guide names two respirator standards. Other states must confirm the standard before it is stated as a requirement.
referencesAtEnd: NT WorkSafe, Guide to working with crystalline silica and crystalline silica containing products, version 1.1 (29 January 2026), confirmed for the Northern Territory; NSW Resources Regulator, Position paper on crystalline silica regulation (April 2025), confirmed as a position paper for mine and petroleum operators.

knowledgeChecks.question: Under the national guidance of February 2022, where does personal protective equipment sit in the control order for silica risk?
options: It ranks lowest and should never be the only protection
It is the first control, ahead of engineering controls
It is equal in effect to isolation and engineering controls
It is not mentioned anywhere in the guidance at all today

knowledgeChecks.question: Which fit-test method does the national guidance recommend for full face respirators and powered air purifying respirators?
options: A visual check only
The quantitative method
A smoke test is enough
No fit test is needed

knowledgeChecks.question: When should health monitoring start, according to the national guidance?
options: After one year of exposure to the dust at work on the site each week and month
Only after a worker reports an illness at the site to the manager or the owner
From the date the worker takes on silica-exposed tasks, including at hire
Only for supervisors and the site managers at the job, the office and the depot

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker's respirator model changes. What should happen before the worker wears the new model?
options: Nothing, because the old fit test still applies to it
The supervisor signs for the new model and the issue slip today
The worker is fit tested for the new model before wearing it
The worker uses the new model for one job only, then reviews it

knowledgeChecks.question: The NT guide names two respirator standards for processing engineered stone. What is the correct statement for a business in another state?
options: The NT standards apply everywhere, so no check is needed for any state or any business at all in Australia
The standards named by the NT guide must be confirmed for the local state before they are stated as a requirement
Only the manufacturer's brochure sets the standard for the respirator used on the site and the whole job
No respirator standard is named anywhere in Australia for this work at all, in any state or territory
